lessons.notes_markdown:
## Welcome: Setup and How This Course Works

Welcome. Over this course you will build a small GPT, a transformer language model, from first principles, and train it to write short children's stories. Everything runs on a normal laptop CPU. No GPU, no cloud, and no prior machine learning needed. You do need to be comfortable writing Python.

### How this course works

Each lesson has two parts:

- A short lesson page like this one, which explains the idea in plain language with code excerpts.
- One Jupyter notebook in the course repository, which is where you actually run code.

The rhythm is always the same: read the lesson page, then open the matching notebook and run it cell by cell. Lesson 2 uses notebook `02`, lesson 3 uses notebook `03`, and so on.

The practice exercises live inside the notebooks, at the bottom of each one. When you finish, you upload the notebook on the lesson page to get feedback and a grade. You learn by running the code, changing it, breaking it, and fixing it.

This first lesson is only setup. Take your time and get the environment working cleanly, because everything afterward depends on it.

### What you need

- Python 3.8 or newer (3.10 or 3.11 recommended)
- Git, or the ability to download a ZIP from GitHub
- About 2 GB of free disk space (PyTorch is the largest download)
- A terminal: PowerShell on Windows, or Terminal on Mac and Linux

### Step 1: Get the course repository

The notebooks and the dataset live in one GitHub repository. Clone it:

```
git clone https://github.com/avisalmon/tinystories-academy.git
cd tinystories-academy
```

If you do not use Git, open the repository page on GitHub, click the green Code button, choose Download ZIP, unzip it, and open a terminal in that folder.

### Step 2: Create a virtual environment

A virtual environment keeps this course's packages separate from the rest of your system. Create one named `env`:

```
python -m venv env
```

This makes a folder called `env` inside the project. You only do this once.

### Step 3: Activate the environment

Windows (PowerShell):

```
.\env\Scripts\activate
```

Mac or Linux:

```
source env/bin/activate
```

Your prompt should now start with `(env)`. That means the environment is active. Activate it every time you open a new terminal to work on the course.

### Step 4: Install the dependencies

```
pip install -r requirements.txt
```

This installs PyTorch, Jupyter, and the few other libraries the course uses. PyTorch is large, so this step can take several minutes the first time.

### Step 5: Launch Jupyter

```
jupyter notebook
```

A browser tab opens showing the project files. Open the `notebooks` folder.

### Step 6: Run the setup check

Open `notebooks/01_setup.ipynb` and run every cell with Shift+Enter, top to bottom. If the cells print your Python and PyTorch versions, draw a small plot, and create a tiny tensor without any errors, your environment is ready.

If a cell fails, the message usually tells you what is missing. The most common fix is to make sure the environment is activated (you see `(env)`) and that `pip install -r requirements.txt` finished without errors.

### How to work through each lesson from here

1. Read the lesson page on this site.
2. Open the matching notebook in the `notebooks` folder (lesson 2 is notebook `02`, and so on).
3. Run every cell and watch the output.
4. Do the exercises at the bottom of the notebook, then upload it on the lesson page for feedback and a grade.

That is the whole loop. When your setup check passes, continue to Lesson 2: Tensors and Shapes.

lessons.notes_markdown:
## Lesson 2: Tensors and Shapes

Everything inside a transformer is a tensor: the input tokens, the embeddings, the attention weights, the output. A tensor is just a multi-dimensional array of numbers. If you can read and reshape tensors, and you always know the shape you are holding, the rest of this course is much easier.

The single most useful habit to build right now: after almost every line, print the shape.

### What is a tensor

A tensor generalizes objects you already know:

- a scalar is a single number, 0 dimensions
- a vector is a list of numbers, 1 dimension
- a matrix is a grid of numbers, 2 dimensions
- and we keep going: 3 dimensions, 4 dimensions, and so on

In PyTorch every one of these is a `torch.Tensor`. What tells them apart is the shape.

### See it: the tensor explorer

Use the interactive explorer below. Pick 1, 2, or 3 dimensions and change each axis size. A 1D tensor is a row of cubes (a vector), 2D is a grid (a matrix), and 3D is a block, exactly the (batch, seq, dim) shape you will use all course.

<iframe src="/static/widgets/tensor-explorer.html" title="Tensor explorer" style="width:100%;height:540px;border:1px solid var(--bg-elevated);border-radius:10px;background:#fff" loading="lazy"></iframe>

### Creating tensors

```python
import torch

a = torch.tensor([1, 2, 3])   # from a Python list
z = torch.zeros(2, 3)         # a 2 by 3 grid of zeros
o = torch.ones(2, 3)          # a 2 by 3 grid of ones
r = torch.randn(2, 3)         # random values from a normal distribution
n = torch.arange(6)           # 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5
```

Every tensor has a shape, which you read with `.shape`:

```python
print(a.shape)   # torch.Size([3])
print(z.shape)   # torch.Size([2, 3])
```

### The shape is the whole game

Read a shape left to right, from the outermost group to the innermost number. `torch.Size([2, 3])` means 2 rows, each holding 3 numbers.

Throughout this course our tensors almost always have this shape:

```
(batch, seq, dim)
```

- `batch`: how many sequences we process at once
- `seq`: how many tokens are in each sequence
- `dim`: how many numbers represent each token

For example, a batch of 2 sentences, each 4 tokens long, where each token is an 8-number vector, is a tensor of shape `(2, 4, 8)`:

```python
x = torch.randn(2, 4, 8)
print(x.shape)   # torch.Size([2, 4, 8])
```

Keep that picture in your head. When we reach attention, you will be tracking exactly these three axes.

### Indexing and slicing

Indexing pulls out part of a tensor. Each index picks a position along one axis.

```python
x = torch.randn(2, 4, 8)   # (batch, seq, dim)

x[0]        # the first sequence, shape (4, 8)
x[0, 1]     # the second token of the first sequence, shape (8,)
x[0, 1, 2]  # a single number
```

A colon `:` means "all of this axis":

```python
x[:, 0, :]  # the first token of every sequence, shape (2, 8)
```

### Reshaping

Same numbers, different shape. This comes up constantly.

```python
n = torch.arange(12)     # shape (12,)
m = n.view(3, 4)         # shape (3, 4), same data
m2 = n.reshape(3, 4)     # reshape is the safe general version
```

Two more you will use inside attention:

```python
x = torch.randn(2, 4, 8)
xt = x.transpose(1, 2)   # swap axes 1 and 2 -> shape (2, 8, 4)

v = torch.randn(8)
v.unsqueeze(0)           # add an axis at the front -> shape (1, 8)
```

`transpose` swaps two axes. `unsqueeze` inserts a new axis of length 1, and `squeeze` removes axes of length 1.

### Broadcasting

When two tensors have different but compatible shapes, PyTorch stretches the smaller one to match. This lets you add a vector to every row of a matrix without writing a loop.

```python
m = torch.ones(3, 4)
bias = torch.tensor([1, 2, 3, 4])   # shape (4,)
m + bias                            # bias is added to each of the 3 rows
```

The rule, read from the right: two axes are compatible if they are equal, or one of them is 1. A mismatch that is neither raises an error.

### Reductions

Collapsing an axis with a sum or a mean is how we pool information.

```python
x = torch.randn(2, 4, 8)
x.sum()                       # one number, the sum of everything
x.mean(dim=-1)                # average over the last axis -> shape (2, 4)
x.mean(dim=-1, keepdim=True)  # keep the axis -> shape (2, 4, 1)
```

`dim=-1` means the last axis. `keepdim=True` keeps the collapsed axis as length 1, which keeps broadcasting easy later.

### The one habit

Print the shape. Then print it again. Almost every bug in this course is a shape that is not what you thought it was. Make `print(x.shape)` reflexive and you will save yourself hours.

### Do this now

Open the matching notebook and run every cell, watching the shapes as they print:

`notebooks/02_tensors_and_shapes.ipynb`

Then do the short exercises at the end of the notebook.

### Check yourself

1. What does the shape `(2, 4, 8)` mean in our `(batch, seq, dim)` convention?
2. You have `x` of shape `(2, 4, 8)`. What shape is `x[:, 0, :]`?
3. You have `x` of shape `(2, 4, 8)`. What shape is `x.mean(dim=-1)`?

Answers: (1) 2 sequences, 4 tokens each, 8 numbers per token. (2) `(2, 8)`. (3) `(2, 4)`.

lessons.summary_he: The linear layer y = xW^T + b: nn.Linear(in, out) has weight (out, in) and bias (out,). It transforms the last axis, turning (batch, seq, in) into (batch, seq, out). It is matrix multiplication plus a bias, and the Q/K/V projections, the feed-forward network, and the output head are all linear layers.
lessons.notes_markdown:
## Lesson 3: Linear layers

A linear layer is the workhorse of every neural network, transformers included. It takes a vector of numbers and produces a new vector by multiplying with a matrix of learnable weights and adding a bias. Almost everything a model learns lives in the weights of its linear layers.

### Recommended watch: linear algebra intuition

If you have not learned linear algebra, or you just want to remind yourself and get better intuition, you are very welcome to watch this wonderful playlist on vectors, matrices, and linear transformations: [Essence of linear algebra (YouTube playlist)](https://youtube.com/playlist?list=PLZHQObOWTQDPD3MizzM2xVFitgF8hE_ab).

### What a linear layer computes

For an input vector `x`, a linear layer computes:

```
y = x @ W^T + b
```

- `W` is a weight matrix of shape `(out_features, in_features)`
- `b` is a bias vector of shape `(out_features,)`
- the output `y` has size `out_features`

In PyTorch this is `nn.Linear(in_features, out_features)`:

```python
import torch
import torch.nn as nn

layer = nn.Linear(in_features=4, out_features=3)
print(layer.weight.shape)   # torch.Size([3, 4])  (out, in)
print(layer.bias.shape)     # torch.Size([3])
```

So this layer maps a 4-number vector to a 3-number vector. The 12 weights and 3 biases are learned during training.

### It acts on the last axis

Feed a linear layer a tensor and it transforms the LAST axis, leaving the others alone:

```python
x = torch.randn(2, 4)   # (batch=2, in=4)
y = layer(x)
print(y.shape)          # torch.Size([2, 3])  (batch, out)
```

This is why our `(batch, seq, dim)` convention is so convenient. A linear layer turns `(batch, seq, in)` into `(batch, seq, out)`:

```python
x = torch.randn(2, 5, 4)   # (batch, seq, in)
y = layer(x)
print(y.shape)             # torch.Size([2, 5, 3])  (batch, seq, out)
```

### Matrix multiplication, briefly

The `@` operator is matrix multiplication. The shape rule: `(m, k) @ (k, n) -> (m, n)`; the inner sizes must match and they cancel. A linear layer is just `x @ W^T + b` under the hood:

```python
x = torch.randn(2, 4)
manual = x @ layer.weight.T + layer.bias
print(torch.allclose(manual, layer(x)))   # True
```

### See it: from drawing to matrix

Use the explorer below. The left side is the classic neural-network picture: input neurons on the left, output neurons on the right, and a line for every connection. The right side is the same thing written as a matrix `W` times the input vector `x`, plus the bias `b`. Change the number of inputs and outputs, drag the input sliders, and hover a line or a matrix cell to see that every line is exactly one number in `W`.

<iframe src="/static/widgets/linear-layer.html" title="Linear layer explorer" style="width:100%;height:560px;border:1px solid var(--bg-elevated);border-radius:10px;background:#fff" loading="lazy"></iframe>

### Why we care

A single linear layer can only draw straight-line (linear) relationships. The power comes from stacking many of them with a nonlinearity in between, which you add in the next lesson. In the transformer, the query/key/value projections, the feed-forward network, and the final output head are all linear layers. Master this one operation and most of the model is already familiar.

### Do this now

Open the notebook, run every cell watching the shapes, then complete the exercises and upload the notebook for feedback and a grade.

ReLU, sigmoid, tanh, and GELU (the transformer's smooth ReLU) are applied elementwise and leave the shape unchanged. Linear, activation, Linear is the smallest real network.
lessons.notes_markdown:
## Lesson 4: Activation functions

In Lesson 3 you built linear layers. But there is a catch: stacking linear layers gets you nowhere on its own. Two linear layers with nothing between them collapse into a single linear layer, because a linear map of a linear map is still linear. To learn curved, real-world patterns, a network needs a nonlinearity between its layers. That nonlinearity is an activation function.

### Why a network needs nonlinearity

Put two linear steps back to back with no activation and they are equal to one linear step:

```python
import torch

A = torch.randn(4, 3)
B = torch.randn(2, 4)
x = torch.randn(3)

two_steps = B @ (A @ x)
one_step  = (B @ A) @ x
print(torch.allclose(two_steps, one_step))   # True - the depth did nothing
```

So without a nonlinearity, a hundred layers are no more powerful than one. Put an activation between them and that stops being true: the network can now bend and fold the input to fit complex data.

### The common activations

An activation is applied elementwise: it takes each number on its own and returns a new number, leaving the tensor's shape unchanged.

```python
import torch.nn.functional as F

x = torch.tensor([-2.0, -1.0, 0.0, 1.0, 2.0])
print("relu:   ", F.relu(x))        # max(0, x): zeros out negatives
print("sigmoid:", torch.sigmoid(x)) # squashes into (0, 1)
print("tanh:   ", torch.tanh(x))    # squashes into (-1, 1)
print("gelu:   ", F.gelu(x))        # a smooth ReLU; what the transformer uses
```

- ReLU, `max(0, x)`: keeps positives, zeros out negatives. Simple and fast, the default workhorse.
- Sigmoid: squashes any number into the range (0, 1). Handy for gates and probabilities.
- Tanh: squashes into (-1, 1), zero-centered.
- GELU: a smooth, curved version of ReLU. This is the activation inside the transformer's feed-forward network.

### The formulas

$$\text{ReLU}(x) = \max(0, x)$$

$$\text{sigmoid}(x) = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-x}}$$

$$\tanh(x) = \frac{e^{x} - e^{-x}}{e^{x} + e^{-x}}$$

$$\text{GELU}(x) = x \cdot \Phi(x)$$

where Φ is the standard normal CDF, an S-shaped curve much like the sigmoid. In practice GELU is usually computed with a fast approximation:

$$\text{GELU}(x) \approx 0.5\, x \left(1 + \tanh\left[\sqrt{2/\pi}\,\left(x + 0.044715\, x^3\right)\right]\right)$$

### See it: the activation explorer

Pick an activation and drag the input to watch what it does to a single number, and to see the shape of its curve.

<iframe src="/static/widgets/activation-explorer.html" title="Activation explorer" style="width:100%;height:430px;border:1px solid var(--bg-elevated);border-radius:10px;background:#fff" loading="lazy"></iframe>

### Shapes stay the same

Because activations work on each number independently, they never change the shape:

```python
x = torch.randn(2, 5, 8)   # (batch, seq, dim)
print(F.relu(x).shape)     # torch.Size([2, 5, 8]) - unchanged
```

### Where this goes

A linear layer, then an activation, then another linear layer: that is the smallest real neural network, and it is exactly the shape of the transformer's feed-forward block (Linear, GELU, Linear). In the next lesson you put a linear layer and an activation together and build a working network.

### See it: adding an activation makes it curve

The same tiny network (one input, a hidden layer, one output) is a straight line with no activation, and can bend into curves once you add one. Switch the activation, add hidden neurons, and randomize the weights.

<iframe src="/static/widgets/network-explorer.html" title="Adding an activation" style="width:100%;height:430px;border:1px solid var(--bg-elevated);border-radius:10px;background:#fff" loading="lazy"></iframe>

### Do this now

Open the notebook, run every cell, then complete the exercises and upload the notebook for feedback and a grade.

lessons.notes_markdown:
## Lesson 5: What is a neural network?

You have now met the two pieces a network is made of: linear layers, the weighted sums from Lesson 3, and activation functions, the nonlinearity from Lesson 4. This lesson steps back from the code to answer the bigger question: what is a neural network, and why does stacking these two simple pieces produce something that can recognize handwriting, translate languages, or write stories? There is nothing to run and nothing to submit here. Read it, then open the live simulator at the end and watch a network learn in front of you.

### The idea in one picture

A neural network is a chain of the two operations you already know, repeated:

```
input -> [linear -> activation] -> [linear -> activation] -> ... -> output
```

Numbers go in on the left (say the pixels of an image, or the position of a dot). They flow through a few layers. Each layer takes a weighted sum of what it received (the linear part) and bends it through an activation (the nonlinear part). Numbers come out on the right: the network's answer.

Each neuron on its own is almost trivial. It draws one straight boundary through its inputs. But stack a layer of them, add a nonlinearity, and stack another layer, and those straight boundaries combine and bend into curved, intricate shapes. Depth is what lets a network go from "draw a line" to "wrap tightly around this spiral". That is the whole architecture.

### Where the magic actually is: learning

Here is the part that feels like magic, and it is worth slowing down for.

A brand-new network is random. Its weights are meaningless numbers and its answers are noise. Nobody sits down and sets the weights by hand; there are far too many, and no human knows what they should be. Instead the network teaches itself, with a loop that is surprisingly simple:

1. Show it an example (this image, this dot).
2. Let it guess, and measure how wrong the guess is. That number is called the loss.
3. Nudge every weight a tiny amount in the direction that would have made the guess a little less wrong.
4. Repeat, thousands of times, over thousands of examples.

No single step is clever. But run the loop long enough and the weights drift, all together, into a configuration that solves the task. The network discovers the rule from the data; you never wrote the rule down. That self-correcting loop is called training, and you will build it yourself in a couple of lessons. For now, the goal is just to see it happen.

### See it live: the TensorFlow Playground

The best way to feel this is to watch a network learn. Google's TensorFlow Playground is a full neural network that runs entirely in your browser, with nothing to install. Open it here:

[Open the live TensorFlow Playground](https://playground.tensorflow.org/#activation=tanh&batchSize=10&dataset=circle&regDataset=reg-plane&learningRate=0.03&regularizationRate=0&noise=0&networkShape=4,2&seed=0.31703&showTestData=false&discretize=false&percTrainData=50&x=true&y=true&xTimesY=false&xSquared=false&ySquared=false&cosX=false&sinX=false&cosY=false&sinY=false&collectStats=false&problem=classification&initZero=false&hideText=false)

It is embedded below as well, but it is easier to use in its own full-screen tab.

<iframe src="https://playground.tensorflow.org/#activation=tanh&batchSize=10&dataset=circle&regDataset=reg-plane&learningRate=0.03&regularizationRate=0&noise=0&networkShape=4,2&seed=0.31703&showTestData=false&discretize=false&percTrainData=50&x=true&y=true&xTimesY=false&xSquared=false&ySquared=false&cosX=false&sinX=false&cosY=false&sinY=false&collectStats=false&problem=classification&initZero=false&hideText=false" title="TensorFlow Playground" style="width:100%;height:640px;border:1px solid var(--bg-elevated);border-radius:10px;background:#fff" loading="lazy"></iframe>

What you are looking at:

- On the far right is the data: a cloud of dots in two colors (blue and orange). The network's job is to learn a boundary that separates the two colors.
- On the far left are the inputs: here, the x and y position of each dot.
- The columns in the middle are the hidden layers, the neurons. Each little box is one neuron.
- The large square shows the network's current answer across the whole plane: the background color is what the network would guess at every point. At the start it is a flat, useless blur.

Now press the play button at the top left and watch the square. Within a few seconds the background color bends and reshapes itself, pushing a boundary out until it wraps around the two groups of dots and separates the colors. Nobody programmed that boundary. The network found it by running the show, guess, measure, nudge loop over and over. That reshaping, driven only by the data, is a neural network learning.

Things to try, this is the fun part:

- Change the dataset using the shapes on the left (a circle, two clusters, a spiral). Press play again and watch a fresh network learn a harder shape. The spiral is genuinely hard; give it time.
- Add or remove neurons and layers with the plus and minus buttons. Watch how a network that is too small cannot bend enough to fit the spiral, while a bigger one can.
- Switch the activation in the top bar between ReLU, Tanh, and Sigmoid, the exact functions from Lesson 4, and see how the learned shape changes.

### The big picture

That browser demo is doing, in miniature, exactly what you are about to do in code: build a network out of linear layers and activations, then train it by nudging its weights until it fits the data. In the next lesson you assemble a network like this yourself, and in the one after you train it to recognize handwritten digits.

And the punchline for the whole course: the transformer you build later is the same idea. It is a stack of linear layers and nonlinearities, trained by the same show, guess, measure, nudge loop. It is just much larger, and pointed at text instead of colored dots. Everything else is detail.

There is nothing to submit for this lesson. Spend a few minutes with the Playground until watching the boundary form feels ordinary, then continue to Lesson 6, where you build a network in code.

lessons.notes_markdown:
## Lesson 6: Build a neural network

In Lesson 5 you watched a network learn. Now you build one yourself. A neural network in PyTorch is just the two pieces from Lessons 3 and 4 wired together: linear layers and activations. This lesson is about assembling them into one object, running data through it (the forward pass), turning the output into probabilities, and counting how many parameters it has. You will not train it yet; that is the next lesson. Here the goal is to hold a whole network in your hands and understand every part.

### The smallest real network

A network is a linear layer, an activation, then another linear layer:

```
input (in_features) -> Linear -> activation -> Linear -> output (out_features)
```

The first linear layer maps the input into a hidden space, the activation bends it, and the second linear layer maps the hidden space to the outputs. The middle size, the hidden layer, is yours to choose: bigger means more capacity.

### Way 1: nn.Sequential

The quickest way to stack layers is `nn.Sequential`. You list the layers in order and it runs them one after another:

```python
import torch
import torch.nn as nn

model = nn.Sequential(
    nn.Linear(8, 16),   # input 8 -> hidden 16
    nn.ReLU(),          # activation
    nn.Linear(16, 3),   # hidden 16 -> output 3
)

x = torch.randn(4, 8)   # (batch=4, in=8)
y = model(x)
print(y.shape)          # torch.Size([4, 3])  (batch, out)
```

Calling `model(x)` runs the forward pass: `x` goes through each layer in turn and out comes `y`. The input's last axis (8) matches the first Linear's `in_features`, and the output's last axis (3) is the last Linear's `out_features`. The batch axis rides along untouched.

### Way 2: nn.Module (the real way)

`nn.Sequential` is fine for a straight stack, but real models, including the transformer, subclass `nn.Module`. You define the layers in `__init__` and describe the forward pass in `forward`:

```python
class MLP(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, in_features, hidden, out_features):
        super().__init__()
        self.fc1 = nn.Linear(in_features, hidden)
        self.act = nn.ReLU()
        self.fc2 = nn.Linear(hidden, out_features)

    def forward(self, x):
        x = self.fc1(x)
        x = self.act(x)
        x = self.fc2(x)
        return x

model = MLP(8, 16, 3)
print(model(torch.randn(4, 8)).shape)   # torch.Size([4, 3])
```

This does exactly the same thing as the Sequential version, but `forward` is now plain Python: you can print shapes inside it, add branches, reuse layers. This is the pattern you will use for every model from here on, including the GPT.

### From scores to probabilities: softmax

The raw outputs of the last linear layer are called logits: unbounded numbers, one per class. To read them as class probabilities (positive, summing to 1), apply softmax over the last axis:

```python
import torch.nn.functional as F

logits = model(torch.randn(1, 8))   # shape (1, 3)
probs = F.softmax(logits, dim=-1)   # shape (1, 3), the row sums to 1
print(probs)
print(probs.sum(dim=-1))            # tensor([1.])
```

Softmax turns the three scores into three probabilities, and the largest logit becomes the largest probability. During training you usually skip this and let the loss work on the logits directly (next lesson), but softmax is how you read a prediction.

### Counting parameters

Every weight and bias in the network is a parameter, a number that training will adjust. You can count them:

```python
total = sum(p.numel() for p in model.parameters())
print(total, 'parameters')
```

For `MLP(8, 16, 3)`: the first layer has 8x16 weights + 16 biases = 144, the second has 16x3 + 3 = 51, total 195. Small. The GPT you build later has millions, counted the exact same way.

### See it: build an MLP

Use the builder below. Set the input size, the hidden layer size (and add more hidden layers), and the output size. Watch the shape flow from input to output and the parameter count update as you change the network. This is the same arithmetic you just did by hand.

Because `MLP` is an `nn.Module`, you get useful things for free:

lessons.summary_he: Softmax turns a vector of raw scores (logits) into a probability distribution that sums to 1: exponentiate, then divide by the total. Covers the distribution-not-a-decision idea, shift-invariance and numerical safety, and the temperature knob that sharpens or flattens it, the same knob used later in scaled attention and in sampling. Interactive explorer plus a notebook.
lessons.notes_markdown:
## Lesson 7: Softmax, turning scores into probabilities

In Lesson 6 your network's last layer produced logits: raw, unbounded scores, one per class. To do almost anything useful with them, to train the network, to read a prediction, or to pick the next word, you first turn them into a probability distribution. The tool for that is softmax, and it shows up so often in a transformer that it is worth understanding deeply, once, right now.

You will meet softmax three more times: it is the heart of the training loss (next lesson), it is how attention decides where to look (later), and it is how the finished model chooses each next word (at the end). Same function every time.

### What softmax does

Softmax takes a vector of real numbers and returns a vector of the same length that is a valid probability distribution: every entry is between 0 and 1, and they all add up to 1. The recipe has two steps: exponentiate every score, then divide by the total. For three scores z1, z2, z3:

$$\text{softmax}(z) = \left[\; \frac{e^{z1}}{S},\; \frac{e^{z2}}{S},\; \frac{e^{z3}}{S} \;\right] \quad \text{where} \quad S = e^{z1} + e^{z2} + e^{z3}$$

The exponential is the important part. It is always positive, so there are no negative probabilities, and it amplifies differences: a score that is a little higher becomes a lot more probable. The bigger the gaps between scores, the more softmax concentrates on the winner.

```python
import torch
import torch.nn.functional as F

z = torch.tensor([2.0, 1.0, 0.1])
p = F.softmax(z, dim=-1)
print(p)          # tensor([0.659, 0.242, 0.099])
print(p.sum())    # tensor(1.)
```

### It is a distribution, not a decision

Softmax does not pick a class; it assigns a probability to every class. If you only want the single best class, take the argmax of the logits directly. Softmax does not change their order, so the argmax of the logits equals the argmax of the probabilities. Softmax earns its keep when you need the whole distribution: to measure how wrong a prediction is (the loss), to weight things (attention), or to sample (generation).

### Two properties worth knowing

Shift-invariance: adding the same constant to every score leaves the result unchanged. This is why, for numerical safety, libraries subtract the largest score before exponentiating, so a big score cannot overflow. PyTorch does this for you.

```python
z = torch.tensor([2.0, 1.0, 0.1])
print(torch.allclose(F.softmax(z, dim=-1), F.softmax(z + 100, dim=-1)))   # True
```

Not scale-invariant: multiplying the scores changes everything, and that is the useful knob called temperature.

### Temperature: sharp or soft

Divide the scores by a temperature T before softmax:

- T below 1 spreads the scores out, so softmax gets sharper: more confident, closer to picking just the top one.
- T above 1 pulls the scores together, so softmax gets flatter: more uniform, less certain.
- T equal to 1 is plain softmax.

```python
z = torch.tensor([2.0, 1.0, 0.1])
print(F.softmax(z / 0.5, dim=-1))   # sharper
print(F.softmax(z / 2.0, dim=-1))   # flatter
```

This one idea comes back twice: scaled attention divides the scores by the square root of the key size to stop softmax from getting too sharp, and text generation uses temperature to make the model more or less adventurous when it picks the next word.

### See it: the softmax explorer

Drag the three scores and the temperature and watch the probability bars respond. Notice how raising one score steals probability from the others, and how temperature sharpens or flattens the whole distribution.

<iframe src="/static/widgets/softmax-explorer.html" title="Softmax explorer" style="width:100%;height:470px;border:1px solid var(--bg-elevated);border-radius:10px;background:#fff" loading="lazy"></iframe>

### Where softmax is going

- Next lesson, the training loss (cross-entropy) is softmax followed by measuring how surprised the model was by the correct answer.
- In the attention lessons, the attention weights are a softmax over scores: that is how each token decides how much to read from every other token.
- In the generation lessons, the model applies softmax with a temperature over the whole vocabulary to choose each next word.

Same function, three jobs.

### Do this now

Open the notebook, compute softmax by hand and with PyTorch, check that it sums to 1, watch temperature sharpen and flatten it, then do the exercises and upload the notebook for feedback and a grade.

lessons.notes_markdown: ## Lesson 8: Datasets and DataLoaders A network learns from data, and real datasets are too big to hand to the model all at once. This lesson is about how PyTorch feeds data to a network: a Dataset holds the examples, and a DataLoader serves them in small, shuffled batches. You will load the real MNIST handwriting dataset and get it ready to train on. No training yet, that comes next; here you just get the data flowing. ### MNIST: the classic handwriting dataset MNIST is 70,000 small grayscale images of handwritten digits 0 to 9, each 28x28 pixels, split into 60,000 for training and 10,000 for testing. It is the hello world of neural networks. `torchvision` can download and load it for you. ```python import torch from torchvision import datasets, transforms transform = transforms.ToTensor() # each image becomes a (1, 28, 28) float tensor in [0, 1] train_ds = datasets.MNIST(root='./data', train=True, download=True, transform=transform) test_ds = datasets.MNIST(root='./data', train=False, download=True, transform=transform) print(len(train_ds), 'training images') # 60000 print(len(test_ds), 'test images') # 10000 ``` The first run downloads MNIST (about 11 MB) into a local `data` folder, once. After that it loads from disk. ### A look at the data Here are some digits from the training set, each with its label above it. They are messy, slanted, and inconsistent from one writer to the next, which is exactly what makes learning them interesting: And here is the key idea: a picture is just a grid of numbers. This single digit is a 28x28 grid where each number is the brightness of one pixel (0 is the black background, up to 255 for the brightest ink). Squint and you can see the 5 hiding in the numbers: After `transforms.ToTensor()`, PyTorch stores these as float32 numbers between 0.0 and 1.0 (each pixel divided by 255), shaped `(1, 28, 28)`. The label is a plain Python int (a 5 here). That grid of numbers is all the network ever sees. ### One example A Dataset is indexable: `train_ds[i]` gives you the i-th (image, label) pair. ```python image, label = train_ds[0] print(image.shape) # torch.Size([1, 28, 28]) (channel, height, width) print(label) # the digit in the image ``` Each image is a `(1, 28, 28)` tensor: one channel (grayscale), 28 rows, 28 columns, with pixel values between 0 and 1. ### Why batches You could feed the network one image at a time, but that is slow and noisy. You could feed all 60,000 at once, but that may not fit in memory and does not help learning. The sweet spot is a mini-batch: a small group, say 64 images, processed together. Training walks through the whole dataset one batch at a time. ### The DataLoader A DataLoader wraps a Dataset and hands out batches, optionally shuffled. Shuffling the training data each pass keeps the network from memorizing the order. ```python from torch.utils.data import DataLoader train_loader = DataLoader(train_ds, batch_size=64, shuffle=True) test_loader = DataLoader(test_ds, batch_size=1000, shuffle=False) images, labels = next(iter(train_loader)) print(images.shape) # torch.Size([64, 1, 28, 28]) (batch, channel, height, width) print(labels.shape) # torch.Size([64]) ``` The DataLoader stacked 64 images into one tensor with a new batch axis at the front. This is the `(batch, ...)` shape you have been tracking since Lesson 2. ### Train and test, and why they differ Notice the data came in two parts, and the two loaders above are configured differently. That is not an accident. The training set (60,000 images) is what the network learns from: it sees these over and over and adjusts its weights to get them right. The test set (10,000 images) is held aside and never used for learning. It exists to answer one honest question: does the network actually recognize digits, or did it just memorize the ones it trained on? That question matters because of overfitting. A network with enough capacity can, instead of learning the general shape of a 3, memorize each specific training image. It would then score almost perfectly on the training set yet fail on a digit it has never seen. The only way to catch that is to measure on data the network was never trained on, which is exactly what the held-out test set is for. If training accuracy keeps climbing while test accuracy stalls or falls, the network is overfitting. This is also why the two loaders differ: - `shuffle=True` on the training loader reshuffles the order every epoch, so the network cannot pick up anything from the sequence of examples. `shuffle=False` on the test loader, because order does not matter when you are only measuring. - `batch_size` is larger (1000) for the test loader because evaluation does no learning and stores no gradients, so bigger batches simply run faster. The training batch stays small (64) because each batch produces one weight update, and many small updates train better than a few huge ones. A habit you will reuse all the way to the transformer: learn on the training set, judge on held-out data, and never let the test set leak into training. ### Flattening for an MLP An MLP expects a flat vector per example, not a 28x28 grid. Right now a batch of images has shape `(64, 1, 28, 28)`: 64 images, each with 1 channel of 28 by 28 pixels. You need to turn each image into a single 784-number vector (1 * 28 * 28 = 784), while keeping the 64 images separate: ```python x = images.view(images.size(0), -1) # keep the batch axis, flatten the rest print(x.shape) # torch.Size([64, 784]) ``` Read that one line piece by piece: - `.view(...)` returns the same numbers arranged in a new shape. It never copies or changes the data, it just reinterprets how the flat block of numbers is grouped. - `images.size(0)` is the length of the first axis, here 64, the batch size. You pass it in so the batch axis stays exactly as it is: still 64 separate images. - `-1` is a placeholder that means "you work out this dimension." PyTorch multiplies the remaining axes (1 * 28 * 28 = 784) and fills it in, so the result is `(64, 784)`. You could have written `images.view(64, 784)` and gotten the same result, but `images.size(0)` and `-1` let the line work for any batch size and image size without editing numbers by hand. A batch of 32 color 8 by 8 images would become `(32, 192)` with the exact same code. Now each of the 64 images is a 784-number vector, exactly what an `nn.Linear(784, ...)` wants. (`.view` needs the tensor laid out contiguously in memory, which it is here; `.reshape` is the safe general version that also works when it is not. Later, for the transformer, you will keep the 2D structure instead of flattening, but for a plain MLP on MNIST, flat is right.) ### Epochs and batches, the vocabulary Two words you will use constantly next: - a batch is one group of examples processed together (64 images here), - an epoch is one full pass through the entire dataset (all 60,000 images, batch by batch). Training usually runs for several epochs, and the DataLoader reshuffles the batches at the start of each one. ### See it: batches and epochs Use the widget below. Set the dataset size and the batch size and watch how the examples get shuffled and grouped into batches, and what one epoch looks like. Notice that a smaller batch size means more batches per epoch. ### Beyond MNIST: where to find more data MNIST is just one of many ready-made datasets, and the pattern you learned here works for all of them: get a Dataset, hand it to a DataLoader, and the rest of your code stays the same. `torchvision.datasets` alone gives you dozens, loaded the exact same way (swap the class name, keep the DataLoader): ```python from torchvision import datasets datasets.FashionMNIST(root='./data', download=True) # clothing, same 28x28 shape as MNIST datasets.CIFAR10(root='./data', download=True) # 32x32 color photos, 10 classes datasets.KMNIST(root='./data', download=True) # Japanese handwriting ``` FashionMNIST is a popular drop-in replacement for MNIST (same shapes, harder task), so it makes a great next experiment: change that one line and rerun everything in this lesson. To go wider when you start your own projects: - torchvision datasets: the full list of built-in image datasets, and how each one is loaded, is in the PyTorch docs at [pytorch.org/vision/stable/datasets.html](https://pytorch.org/vision/stable/datasets.html). The audio world has the same idea in `torchaudio.datasets`. - HuggingFace Datasets: by far the largest catalog (text, images, audio, tens of thousands of datasets), browsable at [huggingface.co/datasets](https://huggingface.co/datasets). You load any of them with the `datasets` library that is already in this course's requirements. TinyStories, the dataset this course is built around, is hosted there too: ```python from datasets import load_dataset ds = load_dataset('roneneldan/TinyStories') # the children's stories your GPT will learn from ``` - Your own data: when you have your own examples, you wrap them in a custom Dataset by subclassing `torch.utils.data.Dataset` and defining `__len__` (how many examples) and `__getitem__` (return the i-th example). A DataLoader then batches it for you, exactly like MNIST. Whichever source you use, the abstraction is the same, and that is the whole point: once your data is a Dataset behind a DataLoader, the training code you write next does not care where it came from. ### Do this now Open the notebook, download MNIST, look at a few images and their labels, build the DataLoaders, and inspect a batch's shape. Then do the exercises and upload the notebook for feedback and a grade.

lessons.summary_he: A loss is one number saying how wrong a prediction is; training minimizes it. Cross-entropy for classification is -log of the softmax probability on the true class, so it rewards confident-correct and punishes confident-wrong without limit. Covers why nn.CrossEntropyLoss takes raw logits and integer labels (not softmaxed), batch averaging, and why you train on cross-entropy rather than accuracy. Explorer + notebook.
lessons.notes_markdown:
## Lesson 9: Loss, measuring how wrong the model is

Your network makes predictions and you can feed it data. But how does it improve? The first ingredient of learning is a way to measure how wrong a prediction is, as a single number. That number is the loss, and training is nothing more than changing the weights to make the loss smaller. This lesson is about the loss used for classification: cross-entropy, which picks up right where softmax (Lesson 7) left off.

### A loss is one number

A loss function takes the model's prediction and the true answer and returns a single number: high when the prediction is bad, low when it is good, zero when it is perfect. Every training run is a long effort to push this one number down.

Different tasks use different losses. For predicting a number (regression) you might use the squared error. For predicting a class (which digit is this?) the standard is cross-entropy, and that is what you will use for MNIST and, later, for predicting the next word.

### Cross-entropy: reward the probability on the true class

Recall from Lesson 7 that softmax turns the model's logits into probabilities over the classes. Cross-entropy asks one simple question: what probability did the model give the correct class?

- If the model gave the true class a high probability, it was confident and right, so the loss should be low.
- If it gave the true class a low probability, the loss should be high.

The formula that does this is the negative logarithm of that probability:

$$\text{loss} = -\log(p)$$

where p is the probability the model assigned to the correct class.

### A one-minute reminder: what is a logarithm?

A logarithm is the reverse of raising to a power: since 10 to the power 2 is 100, the log base 10 of 100 is 2. It asks "what power gives me this number?" In machine learning, log almost always means the natural logarithm (written ln), which uses the number e (about 2.718) as its base instead of 10; the base only rescales the result, so the intuition is the same.

Two facts are all you need here, and both follow from p being a probability between 0 and 1:

- log(1) = 0, because any base raised to the power 0 is 1.
- the log of a number smaller than 1 is negative, and it dives toward minus infinity as the number approaches 0. For instance ln(0.5) is about -0.69, ln(0.1) is about -2.30, and ln(0.01) is about -4.6.

The minus sign in front of the formula flips those negatives into positive losses.

With that in mind, look at what negative log does to a probability:

- -log(1.0) = 0. Full confidence in the right answer costs nothing.
- -log(0.5) is about 0.69.
- -log(0.1) is about 2.30. Giving the right answer only a 10 percent chance is expensive.
- as p approaches 0, -log(p) goes to infinity. Being confidently wrong is punished without limit.

That shape is the whole point: cross-entropy gently rewards moving more probability onto the true class, and punishes confident mistakes very hard, which pushes the model to be both correct and well calibrated.

One more way to feel it: -log(p) is the surprise of the true answer. If the model gave the correct class a high probability, the truth is unsurprising and cheap; if it gave it almost none, the truth is a shock and the loss is large. Cross-entropy is the average surprise of the correct answers, and training works to make the truth less and less surprising to the model.

### See it: the cross-entropy explorer

Move the logits and choose which class is the true answer. Watch the softmax probabilities, and watch the loss, which is just the negative log of the bar for the true class. Give the true class more probability and the loss falls toward 0; starve it and the loss climbs.

<iframe src="/static/widgets/cross-entropy-explorer.html" title="Cross-entropy explorer" style="width:100%;height:470px;border:1px solid var(--bg-elevated);border-radius:10px;background:#fff" loading="lazy"></iframe>

### In PyTorch: pass the logits, not the probabilities

Here is the practical part that trips people up. PyTorch's cross-entropy takes the raw logits and the integer class labels, and does the softmax for you, internally, in a numerically safe way. So you do NOT apply softmax first.

```python
import torch
import torch.nn.functional as F

logits = torch.tensor([[2.0, 0.5, 0.1]])   # one example, 3 classes, raw scores
label  = torch.tensor([0])                 # the correct class is 0 (an integer, not one-hot)

loss = F.cross_entropy(logits, label)
print(loss)   # tensor(0.317...)
```

(`nn.CrossEntropyLoss` is the class version of the same thing: `criterion = nn.CrossEntropyLoss()` then `loss = criterion(logits, label)`.) The labels are plain integers, exactly the ones the DataLoader handed you in Lesson 8. This is why Lesson 6 said to keep the logits and not softmax the output: the loss wants the logits.

### Confident and wrong is the worst case

```python
good = F.cross_entropy(torch.tensor([[5.0, 0.0, 0.0]]), torch.tensor([0]))  # sure, and right
bad  = F.cross_entropy(torch.tensor([[0.0, 0.0, 5.0]]), torch.tensor([0]))  # sure, and wrong
print(good)   # tensor(0.013...)  tiny
print(bad)    # tensor(5.01...)   huge
```

### Over a batch

With a batch of examples, cross-entropy computes the loss for each and returns the average by default: one number summarizing how wrong the model is across the whole batch. That single number is what training will shrink.

### Why not just use accuracy?

Accuracy (the fraction correct) is what you care about, but you cannot train on it directly: nudging a weight a hair usually does not flip any prediction from wrong to right, so accuracy gives no gradient to follow. Cross-entropy changes smoothly with every weight, so it always points the way to a small improvement. You train on cross-entropy and measure accuracy on the side.

### Do this now

Open the notebook, compute cross-entropy by hand and with PyTorch, see them match, watch confident-wrong predictions get punished, then do the exercises and upload the notebook for feedback and a grade.

lessons.summary_he: The engine of learning. A gradient is the slope of the loss for a weight; gradient descent steps every weight downhill, with the learning rate setting the step size. Backpropagation (PyTorch autograd and loss.backward()) computes all those gradients in one backward pass, and the optimizer (SGD, Adam) applies the step via the three calls zero_grad, backward, step. Interactive gradient-descent explorer plus a notebook.
lessons.notes_markdown:
## Lesson 10: Gradients and backpropagation

You have a loss (Lesson 9) that says how wrong the model is. Learning means changing the weights to make that loss smaller. But a network has thousands or millions of weights. Which way should each one move, and by how much? The answer is the gradient, and the algorithm that computes it for every weight at once is backpropagation. This is the engine of learning.

### The gradient: which way is downhill

For a single weight, the gradient of the loss is a slope: if you nudge the weight up a tiny bit, does the loss go up or down, and how steeply?

- If the gradient is positive, increasing the weight increases the loss, so you should decrease it.
- If the gradient is negative, increasing the weight decreases the loss, so you should increase it.

Either way, you move the weight a little in the opposite direction of its gradient. Do that for every weight and the loss goes down. That is gradient descent: repeatedly step downhill on the loss surface. Picture the loss as a hilly landscape and the weights as your position; the gradient points uphill, so you take a small step the other way, over and over, until you reach a valley.

### The learning rate: how big a step

The gradient gives the direction; the learning rate decides how far you step:

```
new_weight = old_weight - learning_rate * gradient
```

Too small and training crawls. Too big and you leap past the valley and can bounce out and diverge, with the loss exploding. The learning rate is one of the most important knobs in training.

### See it: gradient descent

The bowl below is a loss and the ball is a weight. Each step moves it downhill by the learning rate times the gradient. Drag the learning rate and press run: small values crawl, a good value settles quickly, larger values zig-zag across the valley, and too large sends it flying off as the loss blows up.

<iframe src="/static/widgets/gradient-descent-explorer.html" title="Gradient descent explorer" style="width:100%;height:460px;border:1px solid var(--bg-elevated);border-radius:10px;background:#fff" loading="lazy"></iframe>

### Backpropagation: gradients for every weight at once

Computing the gradient by hand for millions of weights is hopeless. Backpropagation does it automatically and cheaply. The idea: the loss is built from the weights through a chain of operations (linear, activation, linear, softmax, loss). The chain rule from calculus lets you get the derivative of the whole chain by combining the derivative of each step, working backward from the loss to each weight. Backprop is exactly that: one backward pass from the loss through the graph, filling in each weight's gradient.

You do not implement this. PyTorch's autograd does. During the forward pass it quietly records every operation into a computation graph. When you call `loss.backward()`, it walks that graph backward and computes the gradient of the loss with respect to every parameter, storing it in each parameter's `.grad`.

```python
import torch

w = torch.tensor([3.0], requires_grad=True)   # track this tensor
loss = (w - 1) ** 2                            # smallest at w = 1

loss.backward()                                # compute d(loss)/d(w)
print(w.grad)                                  # tensor([4.]) = 2*(w-1) = 2*(3-1)
```

The loss (w-1) squared has derivative 2(w-1); at w = 3 that is 4, exactly what PyTorch computed. A positive gradient means: to lower the loss, decrease w toward 1.

### See it: the chain rule

Backprop is just the chain rule applied step by step. Below is a tiny chain of operations. Drag the input and watch two things at once: values flow forward (left to right), and the gradient flows backward (right to left), multiplying by each step's local slope as it goes. The gradient that lands on the input is the product of all those slopes, which is exactly the number `backward()` would store in `.grad`.

<iframe src="/static/widgets/chain-rule-explorer.html" title="The chain rule" style="width:100%;height:420px;border:1px solid var(--bg-elevated);border-radius:10px;background:#fff" loading="lazy"></iframe>

### From one input to a whole batch

The chain above followed a single input x, because that is the simplest thing to show the chain rule on. Real training differs in two small ways, and neither changes the mechanism.

First, we do not nudge the input; the input is data. What we adjust are the weights, so the gradients we keep are the ones for each weight w. The same backward pass computes those: it just keeps applying the chain rule past the inputs and on into each layer's weights.

Second, we train on a batch of many examples at once, not one. Recall from Lesson 9 that the batch loss is a single number, the average of the per-example losses. Because the gradient of an average is the average of the gradients, each weight ends up with one gradient that is the average of what every example in the batch wanted that weight to do:

```
L      = (1/N) * (loss_1 + loss_2 + ... + loss_N)             # the batch loss
dL/dw  = (1/N) * (dloss_1/dw + dloss_2/dw + ... + dloss_N/dw)  # its gradient for weight w
```

So you never juggle N separate gradients per weight. The whole batch flows forward, the loss collapses to one scalar, and a single `backward()` call hands you one averaged gradient per weight. Then the step is:

```
new_w = old_w - learning_rate * (average gradient of w)
```

Each weight gets its own averaged gradient, so each is nudged by its own amount and in its own direction; the one thing they all share is the single learning rate. The negative sign is what sends every weight downhill. Averaging over the batch is the whole point of mini-batches: it gives a steadier sense of which way is downhill for those N examples together than any single, noisy example would, the same tradeoff you saw in the batch-size widget in Lesson 8.

That is one step, for one batch. Clear the gradients, take the next batch, and do it again; one full pass over all the batches is an epoch. Assembling that loop is the next lesson.

### Why every piece must be differentiable

That backward pass only works if every operation in the chain has a slope, that is, if it is differentiable: a tiny change in its input must produce a proportional, measurable change in its output. This is not a detail, it is a design rule for the whole network. Backprop multiplies local slopes, so if any step has no slope, the chain breaks and no gradient can get past it.

It is why the building blocks you have met are all smooth, differentiable functions. A linear layer, the activations (ReLU, GELU, sigmoid, tanh), softmax, and cross-entropy each have a well-defined derivative, so a gradient passes cleanly through them. Chain them together and the entire network, from the input and weights all the way to the loss, is one big differentiable function. That is exactly what lets `backward()` find the gradient of the loss with respect to every weight. This property is so central that the field is sometimes called differentiable programming.

The flip side explains a choice from Lesson 9. A hard operation like argmax, or accuracy itself, is a step function: nudging a weight a hair usually changes nothing, and at the instant it does change it jumps, so its slope is either zero or undefined. No slope means no gradient means nothing to backprop through. That is why you train on cross-entropy, which is smooth, and only measure accuracy on the side. When people design new network components, keeping them differentiable is the first constraint, because a block you cannot differentiate is a block the network cannot learn through.

(ReLU has one kink at 0 where its slope jumps from 0 to 1; in practice libraries just pick a value there and it works fine. The point holds: the pieces are chosen so gradients can flow.)

### The optimizer does the stepping

Updating every parameter by hand would be tedious, so `torch.optim` wraps it. You hand it the parameters and a learning rate, and it applies the step for you:

```python
import torch.nn as nn

model = nn.Linear(4, 2)
optimizer = torch.optim.SGD(model.parameters(), lr=0.1)   # SGD = plain gradient descent
```

Then the training rhythm is three calls:

```python
optimizer.zero_grad()  # 1. reset .grad to zero (gradients accumulate otherwise)
loss.backward()        # 2. backprop fills every parameter's .grad
optimizer.step()       # 3. nudge every parameter downhill using its .grad
```

Why `zero_grad`? PyTorch adds new gradients onto whatever is already in `.grad`, so if you forget to clear it, gradients from old batches pile up and corrupt the step. SGD is plain gradient descent; Adam and AdamW are smarter variants that adapt the step size per parameter and usually train faster. They are drop-in, the same three calls. You will use Adam for MNIST and AdamW for the GPT.

### That is the whole engine

Backprop finds which way is downhill for every weight, the optimizer takes the step, and the learning rate sets the size. Wrap those three calls in a loop over your data and you have training, which is exactly what you build in the next lesson.

### Do this now

Open the notebook, make a tensor with `requires_grad`, call `backward()` and check the gradient against the hand derivative, take gradient-descent steps and watch the loss fall, then let an optimizer do it. Then do the exercises and upload the notebook for feedback and a grade.

## Lesson 12: The training loop

You now have every piece: a dataset served in batches (Lesson 8), a model that turns inputs into logits (Lesson 6), a loss that scores how wrong it is (Lesson 9), and backprop plus an optimizer that nudge the weights downhill (Lesson 10). This lesson snaps them together into the training loop and uses it to teach an MLP to recognize MNIST digits, then measures how well it did. This is the moment everything pays off.

### The loop, in one place

The training loop is four steps repeated over every batch:

```python
for images, labels in train_loader:
    x = images.view(images.size(0), -1)   # flatten each image to 784 (Lesson 8)
    optimizer.zero_grad()                 # 1. clear old gradients
    loss = criterion(model(x), labels)    # forward pass, then how wrong (Lesson 9)
    loss.backward()                       # 2. backprop fills every .grad (Lesson 10)
    optimizer.step()                      # 3. nudge every weight downhill (Lesson 10)
```

One pass through all the batches is an epoch, and you run several epochs. That is the entire algorithm. Everything else is setup and measurement.

### See it: the training loop

Press run and watch the same four steps cycle over batch after batch, epoch after epoch, each cycle making one weight update while the loss drifts down.

<iframe src="/static/widgets/training-loop-explorer.html" title="The training loop" style="width:100%;height:380px;border:1px solid var(--bg-elevated);border-radius:10px;background:#fff" loading="lazy"></iframe>

### Set it up for MNIST

Gather the four ingredients: the data and loaders from Lesson 8, the MLP from Lesson 6 (784 inputs, a hidden layer, 10 class outputs), cross-entropy from Lesson 9, and an Adam optimizer from Lesson 10.

```python
import torch
import torch.nn as nn
from torchvision import datasets, transforms
from torch.utils.data import DataLoader

train_ds = datasets.MNIST('./data', train=True,  download=True, transform=transforms.ToTensor())
test_ds  = datasets.MNIST('./data', train=False, download=True, transform=transforms.ToTensor())
train_loader = DataLoader(train_ds, batch_size=64,   shuffle=True)
test_loader  = DataLoader(test_ds,  batch_size=1000, shuffle=False)

model = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(784, 128), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(128, 10))
criterion = nn.CrossEntropyLoss()
optimizer = torch.optim.Adam(model.parameters(), lr=1e-3)
```

### Train

```python
for epoch in range(3):
    model.train()
    for images, labels in train_loader:
        x = images.view(images.size(0), -1)
        optimizer.zero_grad()
        loss = criterion(model(x), labels)
        loss.backward()
        optimizer.step()
    print(f'epoch {epoch}: last-batch loss {loss.item():.4f}')
```

Each epoch walks all 60,000 images in batches of 64, about 938 updates per epoch, and the loss trends down as the weights improve.

### Measure accuracy on the held-out test set

Training loss tells you how well the model fits the training data. What you actually care about is accuracy on data it never trained on (Lesson 8, the held-out test set). Evaluation needs no gradients, so switch to eval mode and wrap it in `torch.no_grad()`.

```python
model.eval()
correct = 0
total = 0
with torch.no_grad():
    for images, labels in test_loader:
        x = images.view(images.size(0), -1)
        preds = model(x).argmax(dim=-1)          # highest-scoring class per image
        correct += (preds == labels).sum().item()
        total += labels.size(0)

print(f'test accuracy: {correct / total:.4f}')
```

A plain MLP reaches about 97 percent on MNIST in just a few epochs. `argmax` picks the predicted class, `(preds == labels)` is a tensor of True and False, and summing it counts the correct ones. Not bad for straight lines and ReLUs.

### train() vs eval(), and no_grad()

- `model.train()` and `model.eval()` switch the model's mode. Some layers (dropout, batch-norm) behave differently in each. Our MLP has none, so it changes nothing here, but it is a habit worth building because later models do.
- `torch.no_grad()` tells PyTorch not to build the graph for gradients during evaluation. You will not call `backward()`, so skipping it saves memory and time.

### The same loop trains everything

This exact loop, forward, loss, backward, step over batches and epochs, is what trains every model in this course, including the GPT. When you get there, only three things change: the data (token sequences instead of images), the model (a transformer instead of an MLP), and the target (the next token instead of the digit class). The loop itself does not change. You have now built the engine of deep learning, and finished the foundations. Next you return to language, starting with embeddings.

### Do this now

Open the notebook, set up MNIST, train the MLP for a few epochs watching the loss fall, measure test accuracy, and see your own network recognize handwritten digits. Then do the exercises and upload the notebook for feedback and a grade.

## Lesson 13: Embeddings

In Lesson 2 you saw that tensors are how we hold numbers. But our input is text, and a model cannot do math on the word "cat". So the very first thing a transformer does is turn each token into a vector of numbers it can work with. That is an embedding.

### A lookup table of vectors

An embedding is just a lookup table. You choose two numbers:

- `vocab_size`: how many distinct tokens exist (the size of your vocabulary)
- `embed_dim`: how many numbers represent each token

The table is a matrix of shape `(vocab_size, embed_dim)`. Row `i` is the vector for token id `i`.

```python
import torch
import torch.nn as nn

embedding = nn.Embedding(num_embeddings=10, embedding_dim=4)
print(embedding.weight.shape)   # torch.Size([10, 4]) - 10 tokens, 4 numbers each
```

### Looking up tokens

You feed the embedding a tensor of token ids (integers), and it returns their vectors. It simply picks the matching rows.

```python
ids = torch.tensor([1, 5, 2])   # three token ids
vectors = embedding(ids)
print(vectors.shape)            # torch.Size([3, 4]) - 3 tokens, each a 4-vector
```

The ids keep their shape and gain one new axis of size `embed_dim`. This is where our `(batch, seq, dim)` convention is born:

```python
ids = torch.tensor([[1, 5, 2, 9],
                    [3, 3, 7, 0]])   # (batch=2, seq=4)
vectors = embedding(ids)
print(vectors.shape)                 # torch.Size([2, 4, 4]) - (batch, seq, embed_dim)
```

So a batch of token-id sequences of shape `(batch, seq)` becomes `(batch, seq, embed_dim)`. That 3D tensor is what flows through the rest of the model.

### The vectors are learned

The table starts as random numbers. During training the model nudges these vectors so that tokens used in similar ways end up with similar vectors. You never set them by hand; they are learnable parameters, updated as the model trains.

### Same id, same vector

Because it is a plain lookup, the same token id always returns the same row, every time. Two positions holding the same token get identical vectors.

### What an embedding does not capture

An embedding gives each token a vector, but it says nothing about order: the vector for "cat" is the same whether "cat" is first or last in the sentence. Order is added separately with positional embeddings, which you will build when we assemble the GPT.

### Do this now

Open the notebook for this lesson and run every cell, watching the shapes. Then complete the exercises at the bottom and upload the notebook to get feedback and a grade.

### Check yourself

1. What two numbers do you choose when you create an embedding?
2. You look up ids of shape `(8, 32)` with an embedding of dim `128`. What shape comes out?
3. Does an embedding know whether a token is at the start or the end of a sentence?

Answers: (1) vocab_size (how many tokens) and embed_dim (numbers per token). (2) `(8, 32, 128)`. (3) No, embeddings ignore position; order is added later with positional embeddings.
